definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: having the air knocked out of your lungs
second meaning: so thrilling or spectacular it leaves you gasping

explanation.surface: Someone out of puff after exercise insists the sensation is thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as BREATH-TAKING and it literally describes being winded; as one word it is the everyday adjective for something stunning.
explanation.definitionFit: A stunning view or thrilling ride is said to take your breath away, which is the stock compliment for anything exciting.

clue.text: One employed to measure up The Queen?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the straight graduated strip used for measuring lengths
second meaning: a monarch, someone who governs a country

explanation.surface: A tailor seems to be summoned to take the monarch's measurements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure up' suggests a tailor fitting royalty; it is just the stationery item, while the question mark flags the Queen as one example of a sovereign.
explanation.definitionFit: The measuring stick is a school stationery item; a reigning monarch governs a realm, so both senses share one spelling.

clue.text: Caterer cooked with coal and gas?

indicators.note: cooking transforms raw ingredients, and accounts that are cooked have been fiddled into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; 'with' adds these letters to the mix

explanation.surface: A caterer prepares food over a coal fire and a gas burner.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture makes 'gas' look like a cooking fuel; it is the American word for the car pedal.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English the gas is the pedal that speeds up a car, as in 'step on the gas'.

clue.text: Raleigh manufactured product used on crops

indicators.note: something manufactured has been built from raw materials, so these letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written; Raleigh is a British bicycle maker

explanation.surface: A Raleigh factory turns out something for spraying on farm fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crops' suggests farming, but a crop is also a short haircut, which is where styling goop goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A crop is a close-cut hairstyle, and styling paste is a grooming product worked through such haircuts.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, as a verb: to copy someone's words or actions mindlessly
second meaning: a large tailless primate

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like animal nouns, but 'Parrot' is a verb meaning to mimic.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate slavishly is a verb sense; gorillas belong to the great primates, so one short word covers both.

clue.text: One's left by lover hiding drug dependency

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it tucked away inside, so one piece is concealed within another

parts.note: one is I, plus the apostrophe-S
L is the standard abbreviation for left
E is ecstasy
as in 'beloved of all', where 'of' means 'by'
her man is her partner or sweetheart

explanation.surface: An addict's partner walks out, having discovered a secret drug habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drug dependency' reads as addiction, but 'dependency' alone is the definition: the island in the Irish Sea is a British Crown dependency, not part of the UK. L holds the E.
explanation.definitionFit: The island is a self-governing Crown territory whose defence and foreign affairs are handled by Britain, so it is a dependency.

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
rump steak comes from the hindquarters

explanation.surface: A butcher recommends a decent cut of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: With 'cut of meat' just before it, 'beef' reads as the meat; it is slang for a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is slang for a grievance or grumble, and a grump is likewise a fit of complaining.

clue.text: Got to love article on queen infiltrating plot

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside something, so this group goes into the middle of another word

parts.note: a garden plot, as in a flower bed
love is nil in tennis, the letter O
the definite article
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A spy is ordered to win affection inside a conspiracy involving a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got to love' reads as an exclamation, but the definition is just 'Got to'; 'on' places the article after love.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that 'got to' you upset or irritated you, the same as having troubled or annoyed you.

indicators.note: a thrashing knocks things about violently, leaving these letters scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Celtic fans relish beating Manchester United or some other United side.
explanation.walkthrough: Celtic is a Glasgow football club and United looks like a rival team; it is really the adjective meaning joined together.
explanation.definitionFit: Joint action taken by a whole group together is shared, combined effort, the adjective sense of the answer.

clue.text: Mouthy old dons judge addressed in court

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing, so one piece wears the other around it

parts.note: 'm'lud' is how a barrister addresses a judge in a British court
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Outspoken veteran academics are passing judgement in a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university lecturers but is the verb 'puts on'; LUD wears the O for old.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouthy person is brash and noisy in speech, the same as being vociferous or brash.

parts.note: a curt reply is a brief one
a limb is a member of the body

explanation.surface: A brusque member of Parliament takes a stand on something in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, not the House of Lords; the answer is a close fielding position near the batter on the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket names fielding positions, and this one is a close catching station on the leg side of the batter.

indicators.note: what reaches us in hearing is a sound, so the word is identified by its pronunciation rather than its spelling

parts.note: a troop is a unit of soldiers

explanation.surface: A unit of soldiers is having its court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company of soldiers' reads as one military phrase, but 'Company' alone is the definition, the theatrical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre company is a group of touring actors or performers, which is exactly this word's meaning.

clue.text: Climber dealing with a broken limb?

definitions.text: Climber dealing with a broken limb?

parts.words: Climber dealing with a broken limb?
parts.note: surface reading: a mountaineer patching up a fractured arm or leg

parts.words: Climber dealing with a broken limb?
parts.note: setter's reading: someone who climbs trunks and cuts away damaged branches

explanation.walkthrough: A limb is also a large branch, and the person who treats damaged branches has to climb up to reach them.
explanation.definitionFit: An arborist climbs trunks to prune and repair branches, and branches are called limbs.

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a row is a line of things

explanation.surface: A politician cheers the Conservative party line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative line' looks like party policy, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To gloat or boast triumphantly is to show delight noisily, like a cockerel at dawn.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: bundled up warmly against the cold

explanation.surface: Someone is fed up with having to bundle up for winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done with' reads as 'fed up with', but 'Done' is a definition by itself and 'with' is only the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A finished deal is concluded, and someone bundled in coats and scarves is warmly swaddled; one phrase serves both.

indicators.note: something torn up is broken into fragments, so its letters lie in a jumble waiting to be rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman furiously tears up a mountaineer's charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rips' looks like a verb that goes with 'up', but it is part of the letters to shuffle, and 'up' alone signals the change.
explanation.definitionFit: Topographic charts show hills and valleys by shading or contours, which is what a mountaineer would consult.

clue.text: Game flappers not hot for louts

indicators.note: 'not' says this letter is absent, so it is struck out of the word

parts.note: game birds that flap noisily when flushed
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Gamebirds that have cooled down are fed to some hooligans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flappers' suggests 1920s dancers, but here it means birds that flap; game birds of that kind are pheasants.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an insult, the word means coarse, boorish or uncultured people, the same as yobs.

indicators.note: things that are distributed are spread around, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Statistics about plant-eaters' welfare payments are being circulated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Benefits' suggests state welfare, but it simply means plus points.
explanation.definitionFit: Plus points or favourable factors that help someone succeed are gains and upsides, plural nouns either way.

parts.note: a grey day is dull and dreary
an old lag is British slang for a habitual convict

explanation.surface: A wretched crook is sent to prison, since 'bird' is slang for jail time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting bird' sounds like British slang for serving a prison sentence; 'bird' is actually the plain definition, a wild goose.
explanation.definitionFit: The greylag is a large wild goose of Europe, ancestor of most farmyard geese.

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so these letters travel backwards

parts.note: the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force
Enrolled Nurse

explanation.surface: Hospital volunteers look after a nurse who is about to retire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orderly' looks like a hospital porter, fitting the nurse scene, but it is the adjective for tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidy and well arranged, with everything in its place, is the adjective sense shared by both words.

clue.text: Meat and a lot of fancy food as a prize

definitions.text: lot of fancy food as a prize

parts.note: cured pork
'a' as in 'ten pounds a head', which is ten pounds per head

explanation.surface: A raffle prize is meat plus plenty of luxury groceries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' wants to be a selection signal; 'a' is the wordplay and 'lot of fancy food as a prize' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A wicker basket packed with luxury groceries is a classic raffle or Christmas gift, so the basket names the bundle.

parts.note: taken as written
the head is the person in charge

explanation.surface: An officer leads from the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The front' suggests a battle front for the commander, but it just means the leading position.
explanation.definitionFit: Leading or in first place, in advance of the others, is the adverbial meaning of both.

clue.text: Salt firm regret backing foe of Farage

indicators.note: to back is to move in the opposite direction, so the string runs from end to start

parts.note: an old salt and a tar are both sailors
Co. is the abbreviation for company
to rue is to regret

explanation.surface: A sailor's company regrets supporting an opponent of Nigel Farage.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel Farage is the British politician who led the campaign to leave the European Union, so his natural enemy is a Brussels official.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brussels bureaucrat embodies the European Union institutions that the Brexit campaigner spent his career attacking.

clue.text: Charlie worried about queen's old car

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
as in 'what's eating you?', something that ate at you worried you
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Charlie fretted over the Queen's vintage motor.
explanation.walkthrough: C and ATE go together first, then wrap around R.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a decrepit, rattly vehicle is a crate or banger, so an old car fits informally.

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a bed is a base that something is set or fixed in, as in bedding in
taken as written

explanation.surface: A piece of jewellery has a pearl mounted in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' reads as a jewellery setting; it is the noun bed, the base in which something is fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearl is one example of a small round bauble threaded on a necklace string.

indicators.note: 'out' can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are not in their proper positions

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Cows hand out some milky produce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dole out' reads as a phrasal verb meaning hand out, but 'dole' joins the letters and 'out' alone signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: This soft, creamy Italian blue cheese is made from cow's milk, so it is one example of a dairy item.

clue.text: One involved in Yahtzee or Go.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the cubes rolled in that dice game
second meaning: to pass away, as in 'when I go'

explanation.surface: Someone asks which board game a piece belongs to, Yahtzee or Go.
explanation.walkthrough: Go is also a board game, so it looks like the second game in a list; it is the verb meaning expire.
explanation.definitionFit: Yahtzee is played with five numbered cubes, each the singular of dice; and 'go' euphemistically means pass away.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ghostly apparition of a living person
second meaning: someone who looks exactly like another person

explanation.surface: A barman pours a measure of liquor and it turns out to be a double.
explanation.walkthrough: Spirit and double both suggest drinks at a bar; one is a ghost and the other a lookalike.
explanation.definitionFit: In German folklore this is a ghostly twin of a living person; in everyday use it means an uncanny lookalike.
